analysis.one_liner: Ends for-profit immigrant detention, gives immigration judges more discretion, and repeals criminal penalties for entering the country.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 44 House Democrats, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Immigration Subcommittee in December 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how immigration laws are enforced. It would ban the government from contracting with for-profit companies to run immigrant detention facilities, require a judge to review anyone's detention within days of arrest, and presume people should be released rather than locked up. It would narrow the criminal convictions that make someone deportable, let immigration judges grant relief in cases involving old or minor crimes, and repeal the federal crimes of improper entry and reentry. It would also bar state and local police from enforcing immigration law and create a process for certain people previously deported to have their cases reopened and come home at government expense.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants facing detention or deportation — especially asylum seekers, longtime residents with old or minor convictions, and people deported years ago who had US family — gain protections, court review of detention, and a path to reopen their cases. Their US citizen family members gain as well.

how_it_helps.text: Requiring the government to prove probable cause within 48 hours of arrest and giving detained immigrants a hearing before an immigration judge within days, with a presumption of release and the least restrictive conditions possible [S3].

Ending mandatory detention for asylum seekers who pass a credible-fear screening and for many others currently locked up without a judge's review, and requiring bond amounts to be set based on a person's ability to pay [S3].

Narrowing the criminal grounds for deportation and inadmissibility, redefining 'aggravated felony' to require at least a 5-year sentence, and letting immigration judges grant relief despite a prior conviction when family unity or the public interest warrants it [S2] [S3].
Repealing the criminal offenses of improper entry and reentry, so crossing the border outside official ports would no longer be prosecuted as a federal crime [S2] [S3].

Creating a 'right to come home' for certain people ordered deported since 1996 who would have been eligible to stay under the new rules, with government-paid transportation back to the US and their records treated as if they never left [S3].
Prohibiting state and local police from performing immigration enforcement functions and removing immigration-status information from the national crime database [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention companies would lose DHS contracts within three years, and state and local police agencies would lose their role in immigration enforcement. The federal government would bear the cost of operating its own detention and alternatives-to-detention programs and of transporting people home under the reopening provision. Communities that favor local police cooperation with immigration enforcement would lose that cooperation.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit detention companies and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill strips most crime-related grounds of deportation and inadmissibility and imposes a five-year statute of limitations on starting removal proceedings for people previously admitted, meaning someone with a serious past offense could no longer be removed after five years; critics argue this weakens enforcement of immigration law [S2] [S3].
The reopening provision would allow people ordered removed as far back as 1996 to return at government expense, a significant retroactive change whose scale and cost are not capped in the bill [S3].

The presumption of release and requirement that a prior conviction alone cannot justify continued detention would shift the system toward community supervision, which opponents argue raises public-safety and appearance risks even though judges could still detain people shown to be dangerous [S3].

Federalizing all detention in government-owned facilities would require the government to build and run its own facilities within three years, a logistical and fiscal burden, and the bill does not estimate the cost [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers substantial due-process protections — judge-reviewed detention, an ability-to-pay standard for bond, judicial discretion in old-criminal-case deportations — that would matter enormously to the people caught in the system. But its scale is large: it rewrites the crime-immigration relationship, repeals criminal entry offenses, and retroactively reopens decades of deportation cases. Supporters see that as correcting harsh 1996-era laws; opponents see it as gutting enforcement. The bill as introduced offered no phase-in detail or cost estimate for ending for-profit detention, and its breadth made it a heavy lift in a Congress where it had support from only about one in five House members.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee in December 2019 and then to its Immigration Subcommittee in January 2020, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García of Illinois introduced the New Way Forward Act on December 10, 2019, joined by 34 other House Democrats as original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced [S5].
On January 30, 2020, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Citizenship — the last recorded action; the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote [S5].
A total of 44 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit detention companies kept their existing contracts with the government, and advocates of strict immigration enforcement kept the current detention and deportation rules in place. Immigrants facing deportation got no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit detention companies and enforcement supporters

for.name: Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Pramila Jayapal, Karen Bass, Ayanna Pressley, and 41 other House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including progressives, members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and Hispanic Caucus, and some moderates from border districts.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat at the subcommittee level for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that referred the bill to its Immigration Subcommittee, where it received no further action and no vote.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsorship or support for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats, about one in five House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and with Democrats holding the House majority and the Judiciary chairmanship, it was a Democratic committee that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would ban DHS from contracting with for-profit operators of detention facilities and monitoring programs, phasing them out within three years [S3]. These companies' revenue comes directly from holding detained immigrants, so their business interest runs against the bill's release and due-process protections for those people.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would prohibit state and local officers from performing immigration enforcement functions and would bar immigration information from the national crime database, ending 287(g)-style partnerships [S2] [S3]. For agencies that wanted the role this is a loss; for agencies and immigrant communities that did not want local police doing federal immigration work it removes a source of friction.

industries.industry: Immigration bail bond and compliance-monitoring industry
industries.note: Requiring bond amounts be set based on a person's ability to pay and expanding community-based, nonprofit-run alternatives to detention would shrink the market for high bonds and for-profit electronic monitoring [S3].
